analysis.one_liner: Bans the IRS from continuing its free Direct File tax-filing program or any successor.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, leaving the IRS Direct File program intact.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit the Treasury Secretary from continuing the IRS Direct File program, which lets taxpayers file federal returns electronically for free directly with the government, and from building any successor free public filing service [S2][S3]. It was introduced in July 2024 by Rep. Adrian Smith with 18 Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it [S1][S4][S5]. The Congress ended before any vote, so the bill died and Direct File continues.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial tax-preparation and tax-software companies, whose customer base includes the millions of taxpayers who would otherwise be able to file their federal returns for free through the government. Proponents also argued it protects taxpayers from an IRS that both audits returns and prepares them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would permanently shut down the IRS Direct File program and bar the Treasury Secretary from creating any successor free public electronic filing option, removing the government as a competing filing channel [S2][S3].

By eliminating the free public option, the bill would preserve the existing market in which taxpayers pay commercial software companies to prepare and file returns that the government would have accepted for free [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers who would have used Direct File to file federal returns for free, and who would instead continue paying commercial tax-preparation software and services out of pocket. The federal government would also be barred from offering a service it had already built.

drawbacks.text: The bill would end a free federal filing option, meaning taxpayers who used it would return to paid commercial software or paid preparers for a task the government can perform at no charge [S2][S3].

A fair objection supporters would raise: Direct File in its pilot form handled only relatively simple returns and a limited set of states, and critics argue the IRS should not both enforce the tax code and prepare returns, so commercial software still offers broader coverage and features.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit accrues to commercial tax-preparation companies, which would keep a customer base the government's free program was drawing from; the main cost falls on ordinary taxpayers, who would continue paying to file returns the IRS could process for free. The strongest defense — that government filing creates a conflict for an agency that also audits, and that the pilot program was limited — does not address the core effect: eliminating a free public option to protect paid competitors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee after referral and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended, which kills any bill not passed by both chambers.

narrative.text: Rep. Adrian Smith introduced the bill on July 23, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
Eighteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no further committee or floor action of any kind is recorded [S4][S5].
Because no action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill expired without a vote, and the prohibition on Direct File never became law [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers came out ahead: the free IRS Direct File program continues, and commercial tax-preparation companies did not get the legal bar against their free government competitor that they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers keeping the free filing option

for.name: Rep. Adrian Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 9109 to prohibit the IRS from continuing Direct File or any successor free public filing program.

for.name: 18 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to ban the IRS Direct File program.

for.name: Tax-preparation software industry
for.role: Major commercial filers (e.g. Intuit, H&R Block)
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for years against a free IRS filing option, whose elimination this bill would have locked in.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat sponsored, cosponsored, or is recorded acting on the bill, and no vote ever occurred to test broader support [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Commercial tax-preparation software and services (e.g. Intuit, H&R Block)
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the IRS's free Direct File option, keeping millions of taxpayers as paying customers of commercial filing software. Its interest runs against filers who would pay for a service the government offered free.
